key_terms.meaning: A constant added to the weighted sum; the unit fires only when weighted sum + bias crosses zero, so it shifts the decision boundary.
Model unit: output = 1 if Σ wᵢxᵢ ≥ θ, else 0; xᵢ are inputs, wᵢ are weights, θ is the threshold.
wᵢ ← wᵢ + η(t − y)xᵢ, where t is the target, y the output and η the learning rate; no change when t = y.
Two classes are linearly separable if a single straight line (or hyperplane) can put all of one class on one side.
A layer of units between the input and the output; it builds intermediate features instead of predicting directly.
Every unit of the layer receives a connection from every unit of the previous layer; its fan-in equals the previous layer's size.
The function applied to a unit's weighted sum, e.g. sigmoid σ(z) = 1/(1 + e⁻ᶻ); it decides what the unit passes on.
Turns a vector z of scores into probabilities: softmax(z)ᵢ = e^zᵢ / Σⱼ e^zⱼ, so outputs are positive and sum to 1.
L = −Σ tᵢ log yᵢ, where t is the one-hot target and y the predicted probability; used for classification.
Repeated use of the chain rule from the output layer backwards to get ∂L/∂w for every weight in one sweep.
If y = f(u) and u = g(x), then dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx); backprop applies this along every path in the network.
w ← w − η ∂L/∂w; η is the learning rate and ∂L/∂w the slope of the loss with respect to that weight.
Update that keeps a running velocity v ← βv + (1−β)∂L/∂w and moves along v, so it pushes through flat regions.
Optimizer that keeps running averages of the gradient and of its square, and divides one by the square root of the other.
During training, randomly switch off a fraction p of units in each step so the network cannot rely on any one unit.
In deep sigmoid networks the gradient is multiplied by σ′(z) ≤ 0.25 at each layer, so it shrinks towards zero with depth.
Rectified linear unit: f(z) = max(0, z); its gradient is exactly 1 for z > 0 and 0 for z < 0, so it does not shrink the gradient.
Slide a small filter of shared weights over the input and take dot products; the output is a feature map.
Reduce a feature map by taking the maximum (max pooling) or average over small windows, shrinking height and width.
In an RNN, the vector hₜ that is passed from step t to step t+1 and summarises the sequence seen so far.

takeaways: A single McCulloch–Pitts unit already computes AND, OR and NOT, because a weighted sum compared with a threshold is a linear decision.
The perceptron learns only from its mistakes, and it is guaranteed to finish only when the two classes are linearly separable.
One hidden layer is enough to represent XOR and any continuous function, so depth removes the straight-line restriction.
Training needs differentiable activation and loss functions, because the gradient must flow through both.
Backpropagation is not a separate algorithm from gradient descent; it is the efficient way to compute the gradient that gradient descent then uses.
Plain gradient descent is slow and overfits on networks, so momentum, RMSProp and Adam are used together with L2, dropout and early stopping.
Deep networks fail with sigmoid units because the gradient vanishes; ReLU and good initialization keep it alive.
A CNN replaces millions of dense weights with a small shared filter, which is why it works on images.
An RNN reuses one weight matrix at every time step, so one model handles sequences of any length.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to combine a diagram, the exact formulas with every symbol defined, and one worked numeric example, and to connect the training part to the architecture part rather than treating them as separate topics.

bank.q: Draw the McCulloch–Pitts neuron. Show the weights and threshold that make one unit compute AND, OR and NOT, and explain in each case why the threshold works.
outline: Diagram: inputs x₁, x₂, weights w₁, w₂, summing junction, threshold θ, output
AND: w₁ = w₂ = 1, θ = 2, output 1 only when both inputs are 1
OR: w₁ = w₂ = 1, θ = 1
NOT: single input, w = −1, θ = 0
Statement that the decision boundary Σwᵢxᵢ = θ is a straight line
Note that the weights are set by hand, not learned

bank.q: State the perceptron learning rule and explain, with a sketch, why the perceptron convergence theorem holds only for linearly separable classes.
outline: Rule: wᵢ ← wᵢ + η(t − y)xᵢ with every symbol defined
No update when the output equals the target
Geometric picture: each weight vector defines a hyperplane
Convergence guarantee when a separating hyperplane exists
Failure example: XOR, weights oscillate and never settle
Role of the learning rate η

bank.q: Explain why a single-layer perceptron cannot compute XOR, and show a two-layer network with one hidden layer that computes it.
outline: XOR truth table
Proof that no single line separates {(0,0),(1,1)} from {(0,1),(1,0)}
Hidden layer of two units, each drawing one line
Output unit combines the two hidden outputs with OR-like weights
Give concrete weights and thresholds and verify all four rows
Conclusion: hidden units build intermediate features

bank.q: Define depth, fan-in and fan-out of a network. Explain what a fully connected layer is and how the number of weights in it grows with layer sizes.
outline: Depth = number of layers of weights; fan-in = number of inputs to a unit; fan-out = number of units it feeds
Fully connected: every unit connects to every unit of the previous layer
Weight count = n_in × n_out plus n_out biases
Example: 784 → 256 needs 200,704 weights
Why this growth motivates weight sharing

bank.q: Describe four activation functions with their formulas, output ranges, derivatives and one advantage each.
outline: Step / threshold: 0 or 1, not differentiable, used in McCulloch–Pitts
Sigmoid σ(z) = 1/(1+e⁻ᶻ), range (0,1), derivative σ(1−σ), saturates
Tanh, range (−1,1), zero-centred
ReLU max(0,z), gradient 1 or 0, fast, no saturation for positive z
Softmax for multi-class output, outputs sum to 1
Requirement of differentiability for gradient-based training

bank.q: A 2-3-1 network has all weights 0.5, all biases 0, sigmoid activation in the hidden layer and a linear output unit. Compute the output for input (1, 0) showing every step.
outline: Hidden pre-activation z = 0.5·1 + 0.5·0 = 0.5 for each hidden unit
Hidden output σ(0.5) ≈ 0.6225
Clear statement of each symbol used
Comment that a linear output layer suits regression

bank.q: For a 2-2-1 network with sigmoid units, squared-error loss and one training example, carry out one forward pass and one backward pass by hand and list every weight update.
outline: Forward pass: pre-activations, activations, final output
Output-layer error δ = (y − t)·σ′(z)
Hidden error δⱼ = (Σ wⱼₖδₖ)·σ′(zⱼ)
Gradient ∂L/∂w = δ × input to that weight
Update w ← w − η∂L/∂w with a stated η
Verify loss decreases after the update

bank.q: A 5×5 input is convolved with a 3×3 filter, stride 1, no padding. Compute the output size, then compute the top-left output value for a filter of your choice and one 2×2 max-pooling step.
outline: Output size = (5 − 3 + 0)/1 + 1 = 3, so a 3×3 feature map
Show the 3×3 patch × filter elementwise products and sum
Number of weights = 9 + 1 bias, not 25×9
Max pooling with stride 2 on the 3×3 map gives a 1×1 or 2×2 map depending on convention — state it
Why weight sharing reduces parameters

bank.q: A network has one hidden unit with ReLU activation and receives input x = −2 with weight w = 3 and bias b = 1. Compute the forward output and the gradient with respect to w, and state what happens on the next step.
outline: ReLU output = 0 because z < 0
Local gradient of ReLU is 0 here, so ∂L/∂w = 0
Weight does not change on this step
Comment on dying ReLU and Leaky ReLU as a remedy

bank.q: Compare SGD, momentum, RMSProp and Adam. For each, say what problem of plain gradient descent it fixes and what extra memory it needs.
outline: SGD: noisy but cheap update, one learning rate, slow in ravines
Momentum: running velocity smooths zig-zag, one extra vector per weight
RMSProp: divides by running RMS of the gradient, adapts per-weight step size
Adam: combines momentum and RMSProp with bias correction
Memory cost and hyper-parameters β₁, β₂, ε, η
Practical advice and pitfalls, e.g. Adam sometimes generalising slightly worse

bank.q: A ten-layer network with sigmoid hidden units trains very slowly and the early layers barely change. Diagnose the cause, and evaluate ReLU plus careful initialization as a fix.
outline: Backprop multiplies σ′(z) at each layer; σ′ ≤ 0.25 so the product decays geometrically
Evidence: gradient norm in early layers much smaller than in late layers
ReLU gradient is exactly 1 for positive z, so no shrinking
Initialization such as Xavier/Glorot or He keeps activation variance steady across layers
Side effect: dying ReLU; Leaky ReLU or ELU may be used
Alternative fixes: batch normalization, residual connections

bank.q: A network gets 99% training accuracy and 72% test accuracy. Explain overfitting in this case and analyse L2 regularization, dropout and early stopping as remedies.
outline: Definition of overfitting and the train–test gap as evidence
L2 penalty adds λΣw² to the loss, shrinking weights; λ chosen by validation
Dropout randomly removes units in training, acting like an ensemble
Early stopping: monitor validation loss and stop when it rises
Data augmentation and more data as alternatives
How to choose λ and dropout rate with a validation split

bank.q: Compare a fully connected network and a CNN for classifying 224×224 colour images. Count the parameters saved by convolution and explain pooling and weight sharing.
outline: Dense first layer on 150,528 inputs to 1,000 units needs about 1.5×10⁸ weights
A 3×3×3 filter with 32 maps needs only 896 weights
Weight sharing means the same filter is applied at every position
Translation equivariance from convolution
Pooling shrinks spatial size and adds small invariance
Trade-off: local receptive field needs depth to see the whole image

bank.q: Explain how a recurrent network carries a hidden state across time steps, why its shared weights allow variable-length sequences, and what long-term dependency problem arises.
outline: hₜ = f(W_hh hₜ₋₁ + W_xh xₜ + b), same W at every step
Unrolling the network over time
Parameter count independent of sequence length
Backpropagation through time is the same chain rule over steps
Repeated multiplication by W_hh and f′ causes vanishing or exploding gradients
LSTM gates as the standard remedy

glossary.def: A small computing element that multiplies its inputs by weights, adds them with a bias and passes the result through an activation function.
A learnable number that says how strongly one input affects one unit.
A learnable constant added to a unit's weighted sum; it shifts the activation curve left or right.
The step size η used when a weight is moved against the gradient.
One complete pass of the training algorithm over the whole training set.
A small group of training examples whose gradients are averaged before one weight update.
Gradient descent that updates weights using one example or a small mini-batch instead of the full dataset.
A number that measures how far the network's output is from the target for one example.
L = (1/n)Σ(yᵢ − tᵢ)², the usual loss for regression outputs.
The vector of partial derivatives of the loss with respect to each parameter; it points in the direction of steepest increase.
Any penalty or constraint added to training that reduces overfitting, such as an L2 term λΣw².
Normalising a layer's pre-activations to zero mean and unit variance per mini-batch, then rescaling with learned parameters.
A setting chosen before training, such as learning rate, layer size or dropout rate, not learned from the data.
Ending training when validation loss starts to rise, keeping the weights from the best epoch.
The state where a sigmoid or tanh unit sits far from zero and its derivative is near zero, so the gradient barely passes.
Using the same weights at many positions or time steps, as in convolution and recurrent layers.
The number of input positions a convolution filter moves between two dot products.
Extra zeros added around an input so a convolution can keep the output the same size as the input.
The output of one filter applied across the whole input in a convolutional layer.
Reusing a network trained on a large dataset and fine-tuning it for a new, smaller task.
A recurrent cell with input, forget and output gates that lets information survive many time steps.
Encoding a concept across a pattern of activity in many units rather than in a single unit.
A function that converts a vector of scores into probabilities that are positive and sum to one.
Backpropagation applied to an unrolled recurrent network, summing gradients over all time steps.
